text: 6 Lecture 6 6.1 Transpose of a linear transformation continued Proposition 6.1. Let T, S : V → W be linear transformations. Then (T +S)t = T t +St (cT )t = cT t. Proposition 6.2. Let T : V → W and S : W → U be linear transformations. Then (ST ) t = T tSt. Proof. Let φ ∈ U ∗ and v ∈ V . Then (ST )t(φ)(v) = φ(ST (v)) = φ(S(T (v))) = St(φ)(T (v)) = T t(St(φ))(v) = (T tSt)(φ)(v). Hence (ST )t(φ) = (T tSt)(φ) for any φ ∈ U ∗. We get (ST )t = T tSt. Proposition 6.3. Let P = [id] γ β be the change of basis matrix from γ to β. Then the change of basis matrix from β∗ to γ∗ is P t. And we have for any φ ∈ V ∗, [φ]β∗ = P t[φ]γ∗. Proof. By Proposition 5.30, we have [id] β∗ γ∗ = [id t]β∗ γ∗ = ([id] γ β)t = P t. The rest of the proposition follows from Lemma 5.12. Remark 6.4. By Lemma 5.12, for v ∈ V we have [v]γ = P [v]β which is the opposite of the change of basis. Thus vectors are also called contravariant vectors. However, for a linear function φ ∈ V ∗, the coordinate change satisfies [φ]β∗ = P t[φ]γ∗ which aligns with the change of basis of V . So linear functions are also called covariant vectors. Physicists use how components transform under a change of basis to define vectors and covectors (linear functions). This distinction is also important in differential geometry; see, for example, [1]. 6.2 Double dual space The dual space V ∗ consists of linear functions on V . If φ ∈ V ∗, then φ maps a vector v ∈ V to a scalar φ(v) ∈ F . The double dual space V ∗∗ is the dual space of V ∗. If λ ∈ V ∗∗, then λ maps a linear function φ ∈ V ∗ to a scalar λ(φ) ∈ F . Example 6.5. Let V = F 3 and ψ1, ψ2, ψ3 ∈ V ∗ be ψ1(x1, x2, x3)t = x1, ψ2(x1, x2, x3)t = x1 + x2 and ψ3(x1, x2, x3)t = x1 + x2 + x3. We define λ ∈ V ∗∗ as λ(φ) = φ(1, 1, 1)t for any φ ∈ V ∗ which is the evaluation of a linear function at the vector (1, 1, 1)t. Then λ(ψ1) = ψ1(1, 1, 1)t = 1, λ(ψ2) = ψ2(1, 1, 1)t = 2 and λ(ψ3) = ψ3(1, 1, 1)t = 3. This λ is one element in V ∗∗. In fact for any v ∈ V , we can define J(v) ∈ V ∗∗ by J(v)(φ) = φ(v) which is the evaluation of φ at v ∈ V . For example J(0) is the zero vector in V ∗∗ since J(0)(φ) = φ(0) = 0 by linearity of φ. This is true for any φ ∈ V ∗ and hence J(0) is the zero function on V ∗ i.e. the zero vector in V ∗∗. Theorem 6.7 shows that J(v) for some v ∈ V are all possible form of vectors that can appear in V ∗∗. Lemma 6.6. Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field F . Then dim V = dim V ∗ = dim V ∗∗. 30 Proof. We apply the fact dim W = dim W ∗ to W = V ∗ and get dim V ∗ = dim V ∗∗. Since dim V = dim V ∗, we have the lemma. Theorem 6.7 (Double dual isomorphism). Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field F . Define the evaluation map J : V → V ∗∗, J(v)(φ) = φ(v) for φ ∈ V ∗. Then J is a linear isomorphism. Proof. First we show that J is well-defined, that is we show that J(v) ∈ V ∗∗ for any v ∈ V . We need to show that J(v) is a linear function on V ∗. Let ϕ, ψ ∈ V ∗, c ∈ F . Then J(v)(φ + ψ) = (φ + ψ)(v) = φ(v) + ψ(v) = J(v)(φ) + J(v)(ψ). And J(v)(cφ) = cφ(v) = cJ(v)(φ). Next we check linearity of J. For v, w ∈ V , c ∈ F , and φ ∈ V ∗ we have J(v + w)(φ) = φ(v + w) = φ(v) + φ(w) = J(v)(φ) + J(w)(φ) = (J(v) + J(w))(φ). In the last equality, we used the definition of the sum of two linear functions on V ∗, J(v) and J(w). Thus J(v + w) = J(v) + J(w). And J(cv)(φ) = φ(cv) = cφ(v) = cJ(v)(φ). Hence J(cv) = cJ(v). Therefore, J is linear. Next we show injectivity of J. Suppose J(v) = 0. Then for every φ ∈ V ∗, J(v)(φ) = φ(v) = 0. If v ̸= 0, we can extend v to be a basis v, v2, . . . , vn and let φ = φ1 be the first linear function in the dual basis (φ1, . . . , φn). Then φ(v) = 1 while φ(vi) = 0 for i ≥ 2. Thus we have φ ∈ V ∗ with φ(v) ̸= 0. This is a contradiction. Thus v = 0, and J is injective. Finally by Lemma 6.6 dim V = dim V ∗∗, by Corollary 4.16 an injective linear map V → V ∗∗ is automatically surjective. Therefore J is an isomorphism. Remark 6.8. If V is infinite dimensional, then J is in general an injective map and not necessarily an isomorphism. When it is an isomorphism, V is called reflexive and such spaces are important in Functional Analysis cf. [2]. Remark 6.9. Unlike the coordinates isomorphism ϕβ which requires a choice of a basis of V , the isomorphism J is naturally defined out of the structure of dual spaces and is independent of a choice of a basis V . Thus we call J the natural isomorphism between V and V ∗∗ and we regard V = V ∗∗. In category theory, the idea of being natural can be mathematically defined and in that language, “J is a component of a natural transformation from the identity functor to the double dual functor.” This is not required in this course. Proposition 6.10. Let T : V → W be a linear transformation. Then T tt ◦ JV = JW ◦ T . That is V W V ∗∗ W ∗∗ T JV JW T tt Thus if we think of J as the natural identification, then T tt = T . Proof. Let v ∈ V and let φ ∈ W ∗. We compute both sides applied to φ ∈ W ∗. For the left-hand side we have T tt(JV (v))(φ) = JV (v)(T t(φ)) = T t(φ)(v) = φ(T (v)). For 31 the right-hand side, JW (T (v))(φ) = φ(T (v)). Thus JW (T v)(φ) = T tt(JV (v))(φ), for all φ ∈ W ∗. Hence JW (T (v)) = T tt(JV (v)) for any v ∈ V . Therefore, T tt ◦JV = JW ◦T . 6.3 Annihilators Definition 6.11. For a subspace W ⊆ V , the annihilator of W is defined by W ⊥ = {φ ∈ V ∗ : φ(w) = 0 for any w ∈ W } which is the set of all linear functions on V which vanish on W . Proposition 6.12. Let π : V → V /W be the canonical projection. Then πt : (V /W )∗ → V ∗ is injective and im πt = W ⊥. In particular, W ⊥ ∼= (V /W )∗ and dim W ⊥ = dim V − dim W . Proof. Suppose πt(φ) = 0 for some φ ∈ (V /W )∗. Then for all x ∈ V , 0 = πt( ¯φ)(x) = φ(π(x)) = φ(x + W ). Hence, ¯φ = 0. Thus ker(πt) = {0} and πt is injective. Let φ ∈ (V /W )∗. Then for any w ∈ W , πt(φ)(w) = φ(w + W ) = φ(0 + W ) = 0. Therefore, πt(φ) ∈ W ⊥, and so im(πt) ⊂ W ⊥. Let φ ∈ V ∗ such that φ ∈ W ⊥, i.e., φ(w) = 0 for all w ∈ W . Define a functional ˜φ : V /W → F by ˜φ(x + W ) = φ(x). We must check that ˜φ is well-defined: If x + W = x′ + W , then x − x′ ∈ W , so x = x′ + w for some w ∈ W . Then ˜φ(x + W ) = φ(x) = φ(x′) + φ(w) = φ(x′) + 0 = φ(x′) = ˜φ(x′ + W ). Thus, ˜φ is well-defined. Linearity of ˜φ follows from the linearity of φ. Now, for all x ∈ V , πt( ˜φ)(x) = ˜φ(x + W ) = φ(x). Hence, φ = πt( ˜φ). Thus so every element of W ⊥ lies in the image of πt, and therefore im(πt) = W ⊥. By the first isomorphism theorem Theorem 4.13, ¯πt : (V /W )∗ → W ⊥ is an iso- morphism. So (V /W )∗ ∼= W ⊥ and dim W ⊥ = dim(V /W )∗ = dim V /W = dim V − dim W . Corollary 6.13. W ⊥⊥ = J(W ) = W Proof. For any φ ∈ W ⊥ and v ∈ W , we have J(v)(φ) = φ(v) = 0. Thus J(W ) ⊂ W ⊥⊥. By Proposition 6.12, dim W ⊥⊥ = dim V ∗ − dim W ⊥ = dim V − (dim V − dim W ) = dim W . Since J is an isomorphism, dim J(W ) = dim W = dim W ⊥⊥. Thus by Lemma 2.17, J(W ) = W ⊥⊥. Remark 6.14. There is a intuitive way to think of the dual space as the mirror of V . The fact that V ∗∗ = V means if you take the mirror twice, you get back to yourself. If you have a subspace W ⊂ V , then its mirror is W ∗ (strictly speaking it consists of φ ∈ W ∗ extended by 0 to all of V , see Homework 6). And W ⊥ is the complement of W ∗ in V ∗. So taking W ⊥ is taking the complement of the mirror of W . The fact that W ⊥⊥ = W is saying that if you take complement and mirror twice then you get back to W . Theorem 6.15. Let T : V → W be a linear transformation. Then (i) ker T t = (im T )⊥ (ii) ker T = (im T t)⊥ (iii) im T t = (ker T )⊥ (iv) im T = (ker T t)⊥ 32 Remark 6.16. In particular, if T : V → V is a linear transformation, then T is injective if and only if T t is surjective. T is surjective if and only if T t is injective. Proof. Since for a subspace W ⊂ V we have W ⊥⊥ = W , (i) and (iv) are equivalent by taking ⊥. Similarly, (ii) and (iii) are equivalent. Moreover (ii) is exactly (i) applied to the operator T t using T tt = T from Proposition 6.10. So we only need to prove (i). Let φ ∈ (im T )⊥. Then φ(T (v)) = 0 for all v ∈ V . Since T t(φ)(v) = φ(T (v)) = 0, we have T t(φ) = 0 i.e. φ ∈ ker(T t). Thus (im T )⊥ ⊂ ker T t. Let φ ∈ ker(T t). Then T t(φ) = 0. That is for any v ∈ V , 0 = T t(φ)(v) = φ(T (v)). Hence φ ∈ (im T )⊥. Thus ker T t ⊂ (im T )⊥. Corollary 6.17. Let T : V → W be a linear transformation and T t : W ∗ → V ∗ be its transpose. Then we have rank T t = rank T . In matrix language, we have rank At = rank A for any A ∈ Mm×n(F ). Proof. rank(T t) = dim im T t = dim(ker T )⊥ = dim V ∗ − dim ker T = dim V − (dim V − dim im T ) = dim im T = rank T . Remark 6.18. We define rank A as dim im LA which is the dimension of the span of columns of A and thus this is also called the column rank of A. rank At is the dimension of the span of rows of A and hence named row rank. The last conclusion the the corollary is also referred to as “row rank = column rank”. 6.4 Linear systems and Gaussian elimination Definition 6.19. The preimage of a set Y ⊂ W under T to be T −1(Y ) = {x ∈ V : T (x) ∈ Y }. For example ker T = T −1(0). A system of linear equation is of the form    a11x1 + a12x2 + · · · + a1nxn = b1 a21x1 + a22x2 + · · · + a2nxn = b2 ... am1x1 + am2x2 + · · · + amnxn = bm In matrix notation, the equation above is written as Ax = b where A ∈ Mm×n(F ), x ∈ F n and b ∈ F m. In the language of preimage, finding solutions to Ax = b is finding the preimage L −1 A (b). Lemma 6.20. For any y ∈ im T , either T −1(y) = ∅ or there is x ∈ V such that T (x) = y and T −1(y) = x + ker T . Proof. If y /∈ im T , then T −1(y) = ∅. If y ∈ im T , then there is x ∈ V such that T (x) = y. For any x′ ∈ V such that T (x′) = y, we have T (x′ − x) = T (x′) − T (x) = y − y = 0. Thus x′ ∈ x + ker T . On the other hand, if x′ ∈ x+ker T , then x′ −x ∈ ker T and T (x′) = T (x)+T (x′ −x) = y+0 = y. Thus T −1(y) = x + ker T . 33 This gives the structure for the preimage L −1 A (b) being either ∅ or x + ker A for some x ∈ F n such that Ax = b. We would like to to develop an algorithm to explicitly find this preimage. So we would need to consider the following problems. 1. Given A ∈ Mm×n(F ), find a basis for ker A, i.e., all solutions to Ax = 0. 2. Determine if b ∈ im A or Ax = b has a solution. 3. If a solution exists, find a specific x such that Ax = b. The starting point of the algorithm is the following simple lemma. Lemma 6.21. Let P ∈ Mm×m(F ) be invertible. Then Ax = 0 if and only if P Ax = 0 and Ax = b if and only if P Ax = P b. If we multiply the elementary matrix to the right of A then we are per- forming an elementary column operation: A ↦→ APij: swaps column i and column j of A A ↦→ ADi(λ): multiply a column i by λ A ↦→ AEij(λ): replace column j with column j + λ · column i Definition 6.24. Let A be a matrix. We now describe a systematic procedure for solving linear systems by row reduction, known as Gaussian elimination. 1. Pivot selection: Start with the leftmost column that contains a nonzero entry. Choose a nonzero entry in this column as the pivot. If necessary, interchange rows so that the pivot is at the top of the remaining submatrix. 2. Normalize pivot: Multiply the pivot row by a nonzero scalar so that the pivot entry becomes 1. 3. Eliminate below pivot: For each row below, subtract a suitable multiple of the pivot row so that all entries below the pivot are 0. 4. Move right and down: Restrict to the submatrix obtained by ignoring the pivot row and all columns to its left. Repeat steps (1)–(3) until no further pivots can be chosen. 5. Eliminate above pivot: Use row operations to eliminate all nonzero entries above the pivot, we obtain the row reduced echelon form (RREF). Definition 6.25. A matrix is in row reduced echelon form (RREF) if (i) All zero rows, if any, are at the bottom. (ii) In each nonzero row, the first nonzero entry (called a pivot) appears to the right of the pivot in the row above. (iii) Each pivot equals 1. (iv) Each pivot is the only nonzero entry in its column. The non-pivot columns are called free variables. References [1] Lee JM. Introduction to smooth manifolds. 2003 Springer New York.
